title: Contextual Vocabulary
tagline: Year 2 — Words with several meanings and how the sentence decides which one is meant

introduction.overview: Many English words have more than one meaning. "Bank" can be the side of a river or a financial institution; "fair" can mean just, light-coloured or fairly good. Contextual vocabulary questions give a sentence and ask what a word means in that sentence. The surrounding words decide the meaning, so the skill is to read the sentence carefully and test each meaning against it.
introduction.placementRelevance: Contextual vocabulary questions are commonly asked in the verbal ability section of company aptitude rounds and in reading comprehension passages.
introduction.realWorldContext: Understanding contracts, instructions and news reports depends on choosing the right sense of familiar words.

learningObjectives: Use the surrounding words to decide the intended meaning
Distinguish the part of speech a word is used as
Test each possible meaning in the sentence
Avoid choosing the most familiar meaning by default

prerequisiteKnowledge.quickRefresher: A word may change meaning when it changes part of speech (a run / to run; a fine / fine weather).

coreDefinitions: Polysemy: a word having several related or unrelated meanings.
Context: the words and ideas around a word that fix its meaning.
Homonym: words with the same spelling and sound but different meanings (bank, bat).
Part-of-speech shift: the same word used as a noun, verb or adjective with different meanings.
Collocation: words that usually go together; the neighbouring word often decides the sense.
conceptExplanation.theoreticalIntuition: The most common meaning of a word is not always the right one. Treat each sentence as a puzzle: try the likely meanings in place of the word and see which keeps the sentence sensible. The wrong meanings usually produce an odd or nonsensical sentence.
conceptExplanation.visualOrMentalModel: Substitute each meaning for the word and read the sentence. The one that sounds natural and fits the rest of the sentence is correct.

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Substitution test
importantRulesAndFormulas.formula: Replace the word by the meaning and reread
importantRulesAndFormulas.simpleExample: "edge of the river" for bank in "sat on the bank"

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Neighbour clues
importantRulesAndFormulas.formula: Words next to the target word narrow the meaning
importantRulesAndFormulas.description: Look at verbs and nouns around it.

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Avoid the default
importantRulesAndFormulas.formula: Do not pick the most familiar meaning automatically

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Eliminate by fit
importantRulesAndFormulas.formula: Cross out meanings that make nonsense
importantRulesAndFormulas.simpleExample: Remove tolerate in "bank of the river"

mainNarrative: Start from the sentence, not the word. "We sat on the bank of the river" cannot mean a financial bank; the river decides: the side of the river. "He deposited money in the bank" has the opposite sense.
Notice the part of speech. In "She runs a small shop", runs is a verb meaning manages, not moves quickly. In "He paid a fine for parking", fine is a noun meaning a penalty, not "of good quality".

Use neighbouring words. "I cannot bear this noise" uses bear as a verb meaning tolerate; "bear" the animal would not fit with noise. "The board approved the budget" uses board as a group of directors, since a plank cannot approve anything.
Test each possible meaning. For "figure" in "Can you figure out the answer?", the phrasal verb figure out means work out or understand, not a number or a shape.
Be careful with words that look easy. In "He gave me sound advice", sound means reliable and sensible; in "I heard a loud sound", it is a noun for something heard.

deepDiveAspects.title: Phrasal verbs
deepDiveAspects.content: A verb with a preposition (figure out, give up, put off) has its own meaning. Treat the whole phrase as one unit.

deepDiveAspects.title: Formal and informal senses
deepDiveAspects.content: Words like address, content and yield have formal meanings that differ from everyday ones. Read for the register of the sentence.

solvedExamples.title: Homonym
solvedExamples.question: In "We sat on the bank of the river", what does "bank" mean?
solvedExamples.whyItWorks: A financial institution would not suit "sat on".

solvedExamples.title: Part of speech
solvedExamples.question: In "She runs a small shop", what does "runs" mean?
solvedExamples.whyItWorks: Moving quickly does not take a shop as its object.

solvedExamples.title: Phrasal verb
solvedExamples.question: In "Can you figure out the answer?", what does "figure out" mean?
solvedExamples.conceptOrFormula: Treat the phrase as one unit.

steps.title: Phrase
steps.explanation: Figure out = understand or work out.

shortcutMethods.title: Substitute and reread

traditionalVsShortcut.shortcutMethod: Substitute each option for the word and reread; choose the one that keeps the sentence natural.

rulesForApplication: Do not default to the common meaning.

commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Choosing a noun sense for a verb.

placementTips.eliminationTechnique: Remove meanings that clash with a neighbouring word.

selfCheckQuestions: Can I give two meanings of bank?
Can I decide the sense of fine?
